mcq.q: In Flavell's (1979) opening example, how did young children differ from older children when studying a list to recall perfectly?
o: Older children said they were ready and usually were not, while young children judged their recall correctly
Young children studied longer than older ones, but both groups recalled perfectly once they said so
Young children said they were ready but usually were not, while older children who said ready usually were
Young and older children both judged their recall correctly but differed in how fast they learned
mcq.e: The paper: "The older subjects studied for a while, said they were ready, and usually were, that is, they showed perfect recall. The younger children studied for a while, said they were ready, and usually were not."

mcq.q: In Markman's (1977) study, what did young children show about detecting omissions in instructions?
o: They detected only spelling errors and missed the omissions in the content of the instructions
They were surprisingly poor at detecting blatant omissions and wrongly thought they had understood
They detected omissions better than older children and adults because they were less distracted
They detected every omission but did not know how to put it into words when asked
mcq.e: The paper: although the instructions were riddled with blatant omissions and obscurities, the younger subjects were "surprisingly poor at detecting them" and thought they had understood.

mcq.q: According to Flavell (1979), what is metacognition in general terms?
o: An innate intellectual ability measured by an IQ test
Knowledge and cognition about cognitive phenomena
The long-term retention of events that a person has experienced
The ability to compute complicated arithmetic operations quickly
mcq.e: Rhodes (2019) quotes Flavell (1979, p. 906): metacognition is "knowledge and cognition about cognitive phenomena".

mcq.q: Which four classes of phenomena act and interact in Flavell's model of cognitive monitoring?
o: Metacognitive knowledge, metacognitive experiences, goals (or tasks) and actions (or strategies)
Memory, attention, language and reasoning in every intellectual activity people do each day
Planning, monitoring, evaluating and debugging during the whole course of doing the task
Person, task, strategy and learning environment in which the cognitive enterprise takes place
mcq.e: The paper: monitoring occurs through "(a) metacognitive knowledge, (b) metacognitive experiences, (c) goals (or tasks), and (d) actions (or strategies)".

mcq.q: What is "metacognitive knowledge" according to Flavell?
o: A conscious feeling that appears suddenly when we realize we did not understand what we just heard
A list of specific steps memorized in order to solve one familiar type of problem again
A score that a learner earns on a standardized test about cognitive processes
The segment of stored world knowledge about people as cognitive creatures and about their cognitive tasks
mcq.e: The paper: it is "that segment of your stored world knowledge that has to do with people as cognitive creatures and with their diverse cognitive tasks, goals, actions, and experiences".

mcq.q: Which of the following is metacognitive knowledge in Flavell's paper?
o: The goal of memorizing a list of vocabulary words before the lesson ends
Reading a chapter one more time before the exam because you feel unprepared
The sudden feeling that you do not understand something another person just said
A child's belief that, unlike many friends, she is better at arithmetic than spelling
mcq.e: The paper uses this example: "a child's acquired belief that unlike many of her friends, she is better at arithmetic than at spelling."

mcq.q: How does Flavell define a "metacognitive experience"?
o: Any conscious cognitive or affective experience that accompanies
A test result that is recorded after the learner has completed the task at hand
A detailed plan written out before a person begins any kind of intellectual task
A stored set of beliefs about which learning strategies work best for which kinds of tasks
mcq.e: The paper: metacognitive experiences are "any conscious cognitive or affective experiences that accompany and pertain to any intellectual enterprise".

mcq.q: Which is an example of a metacognitive experience?
o: Knowing that it is easier to recall the gist than the exact wording
Believing that you learn better by listening than by reading
Choosing to reread a chapter before the exam
Suddenly feeling that you do not understand what someone just said
mcq.e: Flavell gives: "the sudden feeling that you do not understand something another person just said."

mcq.q: What are the three categories of variables in metacognitive knowledge?
o: Goals, plans and evaluation
Person, task and strategy
Memory, attention and thinking
Knowledge, experience and action
mcq.e: The paper: "There are three major categories of these factors or variables—person, task, and strategy."

mcq.q: What kinds of beliefs does the "person" category include?
o: Beliefs about how much time is needed to finish a task and how many repetitions it takes to remember
Beliefs about the difficulty of tasks and about how much information is available to the learner
Beliefs about differences within a person, differences between people, and universals of cognition
Beliefs about which strategies are effective for which goals in certain kinds of cognitive enterprises
mcq.e: The person category is subcategorized into beliefs about intraindividual differences, interindividual differences and universals of cognition.

mcq.q: "You can learn most things better by listening than by reading" belongs to which type of belief?
o: Differences between persons (interindividual)
Knowledge about task demands
Universals of cognition
Differences within one person (intraindividual)
mcq.e: Flavell's example (a): "you can learn most things better by listening than by reading" is an intraindividual difference.

mcq.q: "One of my friends is more socially sensitive than another" belongs to which type of belief?
o: Differences between persons (interindividual)
Universals of cognition
Differences within one person
Knowledge about strategies
mcq.e: Example (b) in the paper: "one of your friends is more socially sensitive than another".

mcq.q: Which is an example of a "universal" belief about cognition that children may gradually acquire?
o: You should use Strategy A rather than Strategy B for Task X as opposed to Task Y
How well you understand something now may not predict how well you will understand it later
Friend A is more socially sensitive than friend B when guessing the feelings of others in a group
You learn most things better by listening than you do by reading them on your own
mcq.e: The paper: "how well you understand something now may not be an accurate predictor of how well you will understand it later."

mcq.q: According to Flavell, in how many ways can you fail to understand something?
o: Two: understanding too quickly for the content, or understanding too slowly for the time allowed
Two: not attending to the information at all, or attending too much to small details
Two: achieving no coherent representation at all, or understanding incorrectly (misunderstanding)
Two: forgetting content once learned, or remembering one piece of content as another
mcq.e: The paper: "you can fail to understand something or someone in two different ways: (a) by not achieving any coherent representation at all, or (b) by understanding incorrectly, that is, misunderstanding."

mcq.q: In the "task" category, which task does Flavell say is easier than which?
o: Listening comprehension is easier than reading comprehension in every situation
Writing is easier than speaking in every situation
Recalling the exact wording is easier than recalling the gist of a story
Recalling the gist of a story is easier than recalling its exact wording
mcq.e: The paper: "it is easier to recall the gist of a story than its exact wording."

mcq.q: Which strategy does Flavell give as one good way to learn and retain many bodies of information?
o: Studying only on the evening before the exam so that the information is still fresh
Paying particular attention to the main points and repeating them to yourself in your own words
Reading quickly several times in a row without stopping to think or to check understanding
Copying the whole text word for word into a notebook and rereading it until it is known by heart
mcq.e: The paper: "one good way to learn and retain many bodies of information is to pay particular attention to the main points and try to repeat them to yourself in your own words."

mcq.q: According to Flavell, what does most metacognitive knowledge actually concern?
o: Only innate characteristics of the learner that experience can hardly influence at all
Only the ability to predict the exact score to be earned on upcoming tests and exams
Only the cognitive strategies that have been taught formally in schools to the learner
Interactions or combinations among two or three of the variables: person, task, strategy
mcq.e: The paper: "most metacognitive knowledge actually concerns interactions or combinations among two or three of these three types of variables."

mcq.q: How does Flavell say metacognitive knowledge differs from other knowledge?
o: It differs in quality because it is always more accurate than other stored knowledge
It differs only in content and function, not in form or quality
It differs in form because it is always conscious while other knowledge is always unconscious
It differs in storage because it lies outside long-term memory in a separate system
mcq.e: The paper: metacognitive knowledge and experiences "differ from other kinds only in their content and function, not in their form or quality."

mcq.q: In what ways can metacognitive knowledge be activated?
o: By deliberate memory search, or automatically and unintentionally by cues in the task situation
Only automatically and unintentionally, never through any deliberate search by the learner
Only when a teacher or adult reminds the learner directly in words during the task
Only by deliberate and conscious memory search when the learner faces a difficulty
mcq.e: The paper: it may be activated by a deliberate, conscious memory search, or, "no doubt more commonly", unintentionally and automatically by retrieval cues.

mcq.q: In what ways can metacognitive knowledge fail, according to Flavell?
o: It can fail only in young children, while in adults it always works correctly
It can never fail because it is knowledge about oneself and is always accurate
It can fail only when the learner has no motivation at all to do the task
It can be inaccurate, fail to be activated when needed, have no influence
mcq.e: The paper: "it can be inaccurate, can fail to be activated when needed, can fail to have much or any influence when activated, and can fail to have a beneficial or adaptive effect."

mcq.q: What concrete effects can metacognitive knowledge have on cognitive enterprises?
o: It only affects the feelings of the learner without affecting any cognitive actions
It only helps the learner remember longer the information that has been read without changing goals or strategies
It only helps speed up the processing of information during the task without touching the plan
It can lead you to select, evaluate, revise and abandon tasks, goals and strategies in light of your abilities and interests
mcq.e: The paper: it "can lead you to select, evaluate, revise, and abandon cognitive tasks, goals, and strategies in light of their relationships with one another and with your own abilities and interests".

mcq.q: In which situations are metacognitive experiences most likely to occur?
o: Situations with very strong emotional arousal that make calm reflection difficult
Situations that demand careful, highly conscious thinking: novel tasks, weighty
Familiar, repetitive situations that have been automated completely over many years
Situations with no clear goal where the learner just follows habit without thinking
mcq.e: Flavell guesses they occur in situations "that stimulate a lot of careful, highly conscious thinking", novel roles, weighty decisions, and where high affective arousal is absent.

mcq.q: How can metacognitive experiences affect goals?
o: They make every goal unnecessary because the learner already feels certain
They can lead the learner to establish new goals and to revise or abandon old ones
They cause the learner to always keep the original goal despite puzzlement or failure
They only affect feelings during the work and never change any goals at all
mcq.e: The paper: "they can lead you to establish new goals and to revise or abandon old ones."

mcq.q: Which Piagetian concepts does Flavell use to describe how experiences affect metacognitive knowledge?
o: Assimilation and accommodation
The sensorimotor stage, in which infants learn through senses and actions on objects
Conservation and reversibility, the ability to see that quantity stays the same when shape changes
The zone of proximal development, the gap between independent and assisted performance
mcq.e: The paper: learners observe relations and "assimilate these observations to your existing metacognitive knowledge and accommodate the knowledge to the observations".

mcq.q: According to Flavell, how do cognitive and metacognitive strategies differ?
o: The two kinds never overlap because each serves a separate goal entirely
Cognitive strategies are always automatic and metacognitive ones are always deliberate
Cognitive strategies are only for young children and metacognitive ones only for adults
Cognitive strategies make cognitive progress; metacognitive strategies monitor that progress
mcq.e: The paper: "Cognitive strategies are invoked to make cognitive progress, metacognitive strategies to monitor it."

mcq.q: Which is a metacognitive strategy in Flavell's paper?
o: Asking yourself questions about a chapter and noting how well you can answer them to assess understanding
Memorizing the last section of the chapter to be certain of remembering the most important part
Reading a chapter through once more to improve knowledge because you feel unready for the exam
Copying the whole chapter into a notebook in your own words so the content is stored more fully
mcq.e: The paper: "asking yourself questions about it and noting how well you are able to answer them (metacognitive strategy, aimed at the metacognitive goal of assessing your knowledge)".

mcq.q: What does Flavell say about a strategy serving both purposes?
o: The same strategy can be invoked for a cognitive or a metacognitive goal and can achieve both
A strategy always serves only the one purpose the learner originally intended it for
A metacognitive strategy can never improve the knowledge that a learner has already
A cognitive strategy can never help a learner to monitor his or her own understanding
mcq.e: The paper: it is possible for the same strategy to be invoked for either purpose and "regardless of why it was invoked, for it to achieve both goals."

mcq.q: Skimming a set of directions to get a rough idea of how hard they will be to follow is an example of what?
o: A purely cognitive strategy
A metacognitive strategy
A kind of person knowledge
A metacognitive experience
mcq.e: Flavell: "Skimming a set of directions to get a rough idea of how hard they are going to be to follow or remember is a metacognitive strategy."

mcq.q: Which two open questions does Flavell raise about cognitive monitoring?
o: Whether it can be measured with standard tools, and whether it can be taught to pupils
Whether it takes extra time from the learner, and whether it raises the cost of education
Whether it exists in children, and whether it exists in the same way in adults
How much good it actually does, and whether it could do harm if used in excess or nonselectively
mcq.e: The paper asks "how much good does cognitive monitoring actually do us", and "might it not even do more harm than good, especially if used in excess or nonselectively?"

mcq.q: Which example does Flavell use to show excessive monitoring can be harmful?
o: A teacher who asks so many questions that pupils become afraid to take part in the lesson
An adult who sleeps too little each night so that memory and monitoring decline on every task
A student who copies so much that he cannot listen and misses the teacher's explanation
The feckless obsessive, paralyzed by incessant critical evaluation of his own judgments and decisions
mcq.e: The paper: "Think of the feckless obsessive, paralyzed by incessant critical evaluation of his own judgments and decisions."

mcq.q: What is Flavell's conclusion about the amount of cognitive monitoring in the world?
o: Overall there is just enough at every age, so no educational intervention is needed
Overall there is far too much, especially among adults who overthink their own learning
Overall there is far too little rather than enough or too much, especially among children
No conclusion is possible because there is no research at all on cognitive monitoring
mcq.e: The paper: "I am absolutely convinced that there is, overall, far too little rather than enough or too much cognitive monitoring in this world... especially true for children."

mcq.q: What did Brown, Campione and Barclay (cited by Flavell) train children of mental age 8 to do, and what happened a year later?
o: Basic mathematics; a year later the children's math scores had doubled
Note-taking strategies; a year later the strategies could be used only in the old task
Self-testing strategies for readiness to recall; a year later the children used them spontaneously
Speed-reading strategies; a year later the children had completely forgotten the strategies
mcq.e: The paper: a year later the subjects "spontaneously used these metacognitive strategies" and applied modifications to recalling the gist of prose passages.

mcq.q: What is the main purpose of Garner and Alexander's (1989) article?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: To report the results of an experiment that trained a reading strategy in elementary pupils
To summarize "facts" from recent research and pose four questions to be answered empirically
To present a new instrument that measures young children's metacognition with structured interviews
To criticize the whole concept of metacognition as impossible to test scientifically
mcq.e: The abstract: it summarizes "facts" emerging from recent research and explanations from metacognitive theory, and suggests four questions to be addressed empirically.

mcq.q: What are Garner and Alexander's four empirical questions?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: Measuring intelligence, measuring short-term memory, measuring attention and measuring vocabulary
Age of onset of metacognition, gender differences, cultural influences and economic influences
Cost of teacher training, teaching time, school facilities and teachers' pay
Measuring "knowing about knowing", measuring strategy instruction effects, content
mcq.e: The abstract lists (a) measuring "knowing about knowing", (b) measuring effects of strategy instruction, (c) relations between content and strategy knowledge, (d) role of achievement motivation.

mcq.q: What is the first "fact" about metacognition the article names?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: "Knowing about knowing" develops with age and experience
"Knowing about knowing" is entirely innate and does not change over time
"Knowing about knowing" exists only in well-educated adults
"Knowing about knowing" appears only after adolescence has begun
mcq.e: The paper: "'knowing about knowing' develops with age and experience."

mcq.q: What are Kreutzer, Leonard and Flavell (1975) cited for?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: Younger children plan better than older children when preparing for retrieval
Children of all ages plan equally when they prepare for retrieval of a list
Older children make more plans than younger children when preparing for retrieval
Younger children almost never plan even when reminded before they must recall
mcq.e: The paper: "older children make more plans than younger children in preparing for retrieval".

mcq.q: What are Myers and Paris (1978) cited for?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: Young children report more strategies than adults when their own comprehension fails
Young children never fail to understand because they only do very simple tasks
Young children always know to reread when they do not understand a text
Young children often cannot report any strategy they might use when comprehension fails
mcq.e: The paper: "young children often cannot report any strategy they might employ when comprehension fails".

mcq.q: According to Garner and Alexander, why is young children's metacognitive knowledge limited?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: It is abstracted from years of experience in the domain of thinking, and young children are novices there
Young children do not yet have a long-term memory in which to store any knowledge about cognition
Young children cannot speak yet, so they cannot have any knowledge about their own intellectual activity
Young children are forbidden by adults to think about learning, so this knowledge cannot develop
mcq.e: The paper cites Flavell (1985): like other knowledge it is abstracted from years of experience; "young children are novices in many other domains, they are novices in this one".

mcq.q: What is the second "fact" the article names?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: Only children fail to monitor their cognitions, while adults always monitor very well
Only poorly educated adults fail to monitor, while educated people always monitor well
Both children and adults often fail to monitor their cognitions
Adults always monitor their cognitions better than children on every listening and reading task
mcq.e: The paper: "both children and adults often fail to monitor their cognitions"; more among younger and less skilled listeners and readers but quite frequent at all ages.

mcq.q: What example does Markman (1981) use to illustrate the danger of failing to monitor?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: When she reads aloud she often misreads the intonation so listeners cannot follow the author
When her mind wanders while reading, she understands less and less but keeps turning pages
When she reads in the evening she soon falls asleep and never finishes any book she starts
When she reads too quickly she skips many new words and must look them up on each page
mcq.e: The paper: if she keeps turning pages, she is "engaging in profitless activity - 'reading' without understanding."

mcq.q: What does Baker (1984) show about children's criteria for understanding text?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: They rely only on the teacher's opinion to decide whether they have understood the lesson
They rely on very many criteria at once, including consistency with experience and other parts
They often rely on a single criterion: understanding of individual words
They rely only on the illustrations that accompany the text to decide if they understood
mcq.e: The paper: younger and poorer readers "often rely on a single criterion for textual understanding: understanding of individual words."

mcq.q: Why do people seldom ask themselves "Am I understanding this?" as they work?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: Teachers often forbid pupils from stopping in the middle of a task to think about it
Asking oneself is regarded as a sign of low confidence, so most people avoid doing it
Understanding always happens automatically and cannot be wrong, so checking is unnecessary
Understanding admits of degrees, we do not always need deep understanding, and we seldom stop to ask
mcq.e: The paper: "understanding admits of degrees" (Markman), and "we seldom complete tasks by stopping periodically to inquire of ourselves, 'Am I understanding this?'"

mcq.q: Which conditions make cognitive monitoring more likely?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: An important task, attention and memory resources not strained
The learner is doing several things at once, so attention is divided equally among them
The learner is under heavy time pressure and attention resources are stretched to the limit
An unimportant task done very quickly, with little need for the learner to concentrate
mcq.e: The paper: "attention and memory resources must not be strained. The task should be important, and the learner should be devoting conscious attention to it."

mcq.q: Whom does Flavell (1981) name as people who usually treat messages as analyzable cognitive objects?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: Young children and novices, since they look closely at every word of a message they receive
Manual workers, since they are used to checking instructions before they do any operation
Scholars, lawyers and other "extremely analytical scrutinizers of messages"
High-achieving elementary students, since they are used to checking messages sentence by sentence
mcq.e: The paper: "scholars, lawyers, and other 'extremely analytical scrutinizers of messages' usually treat messages as analyzable cognitive objects, but it appears that most other children and adults do not."

mcq.q: What is the third "fact" about strategies?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: Strategies are used only when there is a clear external reward, never for intrinsic reasons
No strategy can be taught, so learners can only discover them through their own experience
Some strategies are difficult to learn and easy to abandon; some appear without instruction
Every strategy appears without instruction and learners never abandon a strategy once it is used
mcq.e: The paper: strategies "are sometimes acquired without direct instruction, sometimes only with extensive instruction", and some well taught ones are scarcely maintained when instruction ceases.

mcq.q: Which two "academic" strategies are not used spontaneously by many students?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: Making margin notes and drawing mind maps that summarize the main ideas of the chapter
Text reinspection (rereading) and text summarization
Studying in groups with classmates and asking the teacher when a point is unclear
Memorizing paragraph by paragraph and copying the lesson many times in an exercise book
mcq.e: The paper: "Two 'academic' strategies that are not employed spontaneously by many students are text reinspection and text summarization."

mcq.q: Asked why they do not reread a text to find answers, what do students usually say?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: That it is "illegal" or that it takes too much time
That they cannot read the words, so there is no way to find the answer in the text
That they already remembered all of the content, so rereading the text was not needed
That the teacher had forbidden the use of books during the test the pupils were taking
mcq.e: The paper: "they usually report either that 'it is illegal' or that it takes too much time."

mcq.q: What explanation does the paper give for well-taught strategies being abandoned once instruction stops?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: Variability in the color of the materials
Variability in learner motivation
Variability in the handwriting of the teacher
Variability in the length of the lesson
mcq.e: The paper: "Surely one explanation... is variability in learner motivation. Unless someone wants to accomplish a particular goal, it is unlikely that he or she will expend time and effort to engage in strategies."

mcq.q: According to Peterson and Swing (1983), why do students seldom bring unpracticed strategies into classroom problem solving?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: Classrooms are so quiet that students lose concentration and cannot use any strategy at all
Strategies always lower students' final grades on every kind of test that they take
Teachers ask students to work slowly to think carefully, which makes new strategies unnecessary
Classrooms are frenetic, and using non-automated strategies would slow task completion
mcq.e: The paper: classrooms are "frenetic places", where "task completion is sometimes valued more than effective performance".

mcq.q: What does low self-efficacy (Bandura 1977) do to learners, according to the paper?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: Makes them quickly set higher goals in order to prove their ability to themselves and others
Makes them try many times harder, believing effort will surely produce the outcomes they want
Makes them unwilling to start or persist at problem-solving because they expect not to produce outcomes
Makes them switch to using more complicated strategies to compensate for their low confidence
mcq.e: The paper: the student "is then unwilling to initiate or persist at problem-solving behaviors because of this perception of low self-efficacy."

mcq.q: According to the paper, which factor may influence behavior more than task incentives or actual personal skill?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: The number of homework assignments a teacher gives students in each week at school
The learner's perception of their own ability to perform the task
The color and layout of the learning materials handed out to the students in the class
The size of the classroom and the number of students present in it during each lesson
mcq.e: The paper: "one's perception of one's ability to perform a task may be a more critical influence on behavior than task incentives or actual personal skill."

mcq.q: Which three internal factors help students invoke complex cognitive and metacognitive routines?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: Many friends, many books and plenty of free time in which to study alone at home
A good memory, fast reflexes and a loud voice when speaking in front of the whole class
High self-esteem, an internal locus of control, and the tendency to attribute success to effort
High marks, low tuition fees and a large class size so that many peers compete together
mcq.e: The paper: "Without high self-esteem, an internal locus of control, and the tendency to attribute success to effort, students are unlikely to invoke complex cognitive and metacognitive routines".

mcq.q: What is the first problem in measuring "knowing about knowing" by interview?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: Lack of awareness of processing, given repetition and at least partial automation of processes
The interview questions are always so easy that they cannot separate high and low metacognition
The interviewer is so strict that the interviewee is frightened and does not dare speak honestly
The interviewees like to talk so much that they answer at length without getting to the point
mcq.e: The paper lists: "(a) lack of awareness of processing, given repetition and at least partial automation of processes".

mcq.q: What did Nisbett and Wilson call glib talk about processes that are not really understood?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: "Thinking about thinking"
"Telling more than we can know"
"Knowing more than we can tell"
"Learning how to learn"
mcq.e: The paper: "Nisbett & Wilson, 1977, called this 'telling more than we can know,' the reverse of the first and second problems that might be labelled knowing more than we can tell".

mcq.q: What is the fourth problem with directed interview probes?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: Respondents refuse to answer any of the questions that the investigator poses to them
Respondents speak so slowly that the interview lasts longer than the time planned in advance
Respondents try to decide what the investigator wants to hear and answer accordingly
Respondents have no time, so they answer only a few questions quickly and then leave
mcq.e: The paper: "responses to specific, directed probes that indicate that the respondent has tried to decide what the investigator wants to hear and has answered accordingly."

mcq.q: What general remedy do Garner and Alexander propose for measuring "knowing about knowing"?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: Give up direct measurement and rely only on teachers' subjective impressions of the pupils
Use multiple methods that do not share a source of error so they converge on an answer
Use only shorter questionnaires so that learners do not become tired and lose patience
Use only longer interviews so that children have more time to talk about their learning
mcq.e: The paper: "using multiple methods that do not share the same source of error is imperative", quoting Kail and Bisanz: hypotheses need "multiple methods that independently converge on an answer".

mcq.q: Which is an example of nonverbal observable data named in the paper?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: Eye movements and underlined text
End-of-term exam scores
Long interview answers
Self-completed questionnaires
mcq.e: The paper: "Eye movements are one example of observable, nonverbal data... Underlined text is another."

mcq.q: What limitations of the think-aloud method does the paper mention?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: It is always more expensive than every other method and needs special laboratory equipment
It can only be used with children under three years old and cannot be applied to older learners
Masses of data to categorize, risk of cueing responses, automated processes stay inaccessible
It yields no data at all about thinking because people cannot speak aloud while working
mcq.e: The paper: masses of data, "investigators must be cautious not to cue particular responses, and automated processes remain inaccessible", and reporting may be disruptive.

mcq.q: In the cross-age tutoring studies by Garner and colleagues, what were the tutored younger children trained to do?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: Memorize the whole text before the tutoring session began so they could answer any question
Feign strategy deficits, for example not answering and not looking back at the text until prompted
Read the text aloud to the tutor sentence by sentence so the tutor could note reading errors
Play the role of the teacher and grade the tutor to see whether the tutor taught correctly
mcq.e: The paper: "We trained our tutored students to feign strategy deficits. For instance, they were trained not to answer questions and not to look back to text, awaiting a prompt from tutors to do so."

mcq.q: Why do Paris and colleagues think standardized reading tests are unsuitable for measuring strategy instruction?
mcq.sec: Garner and Alexander 1989: facts and open questions
o: They are designed only for elementary pupils and so do not suit older students at all
They are so easy that all students earn the maximum score and no groups can be distinguished
They are always scored incorrectly, so results cannot be used to compare strategy programs
They are built to discriminate among students on generalized traits, correlate with intelligence

By forbidding participants from observing and evaluating their own cognition during the task
By using brain-activity recording devices instead of observers to remove subjectivity entirely
mcq.e: The paper: "the paradox could be solved by construing of behavior and metacognition as occurring at separable levels of analysis."

mcq.q: What does the sentence "Thiss sentence contains threee errors." illustrate?
o: Readers always overlook spelling errors because they attend only to the overall meaning
Spelling errors do not matter because they do not affect understanding of the sentence
Long sentences always confuse readers more than short and simple sentences do
One error (claiming three errors when there are two) exists on a different level from the errors in the text
mcq.e: The paper: two errors are in the text, but the claim of three errors is an error "on a different level of analysis from the errors embedded in the text."

mcq.q: Does the Nelson and Narens framework assume the meta-level is always accurate?
o: Yes; in this framework the meta-level is always perfectly accurate about the object level
No; the participant can be treated as an imperfect measuring device of their own cognition
Yes; the meta-level is accurate only if the learner has above-average intelligence
It is never mentioned in the paper, which discusses only absolute accuracy measures
mcq.e: The paper quotes Nelson (1996): "the individual participant can be treated as an imperfect measuring device of his or her own cognitions".

mcq.q: What is "absolute accuracy" (calibration)?
o: The number of correct answers on a test
The overall correspondence between judgment and performance
The degree to which judgments discriminate correct from incorrect outcomes
The response time of the learner
mcq.e: The paper: "Absolute accuracy (sometimes termed calibration) refers to the overall correspondence between judgment and performance."

mcq.q: What is "relative accuracy" (resolution)?
o: The speed with which a participant makes a judgment after viewing the content once
The number of judgments that a participant makes during the whole learning task
The degree to which judgments distinguish between correct and incorrect outcomes
The average gap between the learner's confidence and the score the learner actually gets
mcq.e: The paper: "relative accuracy refers only to the degree to which judgments distinguish or discriminate between outcomes."

mcq.q: Which statistic is commonly used to measure relative accuracy?
o: The arithmetic mean of all judgments the participant made in the whole task
The Goodman–Kruskal gamma correlation between judgment and outcome
The total number of errors that the participant made on all the questions of the test
The standard deviation of the scores that the participant earned on the questions
mcq.e: The paper: "Much of the experimental literature favors the nonparametric Goodman–Kruskal g correlation because it assumes that judgments are ordinal".

mcq.q: What did Foster and colleagues (2017) observe across 13 exams?
o: Predictions exactly equal to actual scores on every exam, meaning students judged accurately
Mean prediction 84.44%, mean score 77.69%: overconfidence that was stable across exams
Predictions that changed randomly from exam to exam, following no trend of any kind
Predictions lower than actual scores on every exam, meaning students were always underconfident
mcq.e: The paper: "students' average prediction was 84.44%, and their average score was 77.69%... overconfidence held for postdictions and for predictions of next exam performance and remained stable across all 13 exams."

mcq.q: By how many percentage points were students overconfident in the Foster and colleagues data?
o: About 6.75 points, roughly 7
About 0 points
About 84 points
About 77 points
mcq.e: 84.44 minus 77.69 is 6.75; the paper says "approximately 7 percentage points".

mcq.q: What g correlation between confidence and accuracy did Koriat and Goldsmith (1996) report?
mcq.e: The paper: "The g correlation between assessed confidence and the accuracy was .87".

mcq.q: What does g = .87 in Koriat and Goldsmith show?
o: Participants were always overconfident on every answer whether it was right or wrong
Participants were always underconfident on every answer whether it was right or wrong
Participants could not tell their correct answers from their incorrect answers at all
Strong relative accuracy: judgments discriminated well between correct and incorrect answers
mcq.e: The paper: judgment magnitude was greater for correct and lower for incorrect answers, "indicating that... this relation was strong."

mcq.q: What is one limitation of absolute accuracy that the paper names?
o: It cannot be computed by any formula because judgments have no units of measurement
Changes in performance can alter absolute accuracy without any change in judgment
It always comes out equal to zero because judgments always match actual performance
It can be used only with children because adults cannot judge their own learning
mcq.e: The paper: if judgment stays the same while performance improves on a second exam, absolute accuracy improves, though not necessarily because of better monitoring.

mcq.q: Which assumption of absolute accuracy measures remains an open question?
o: That participants always know the correct answer to every question before they judge it
That participants never guess but always rely on firm knowledge when they answer questions
That participants can map their monitoring experience onto the scale used (often percentage)
That participants always finish every question, so all judgments are complete and comparable
mcq.e: The paper: "measures of absolute accuracy make the assumption that participants can effectively map their psychological experience of monitoring onto the scale used... Whether this assumption is justified remains an open question."

mcq.q: In Rhodes and Castel's (2009) loudness experiment, what did participants predict?
o: That they would remember more loud words than normal-volume words
They made no predictions
That they would remember more normal-volume words than loud words
That they would remember both kinds equally
mcq.e: The paper: "participants predicted they would remember more loud words than normal words."

mcq.q: What was the actual memory result in the loudness experiment?
o: No difference between loud and normal words
Loud words were remembered clearly better
Normal words were remembered clearly better
Nobody remembered any words
mcq.e: The paper: "no difference in actual memory performance emerged, suggesting that participants' confidence in the memorability of loud words was an illusion."

mcq.q: In the second loudness experiment, what was the consequence of the illusion?
o: Participants chose words to restudy completely at random, with no link to any impression they had
Participants chose to restudy no words at all because they believed they had learned every one of them
Participants chose to restudy normal words nearly twice as often as loud words despite equal memory
Participants chose to restudy loud words more often because they believed loud words are forgotten easily
mcq.e: The paper: "participants were nearly twice as likely to indicate that they should restudy a normal word, even though there was no difference in objective memory performance".

mcq.q: What does the loudness experiment show about the relation between monitoring and control?
o: Control determines monitoring, not the other way around, in every kind of learning task
Monitoring has a causal impact on control, so the accuracy of monitoring matters greatly
Monitoring and control are entirely independent, so accuracy of monitoring does not matter
An illusion in monitoring has no effect on the learning decisions that participants make
mcq.e: The paper: "monitoring processes seem to have a causal impact on control over cognition. Framed within this perspective... the accuracy of metacognition becomes even more important."

mcq.q: How does Rhodes describe the Dunning–Kruger effect?
o: The worst performers are always underconfident and estimate below their actual performance
The worst performers misjudge their own performance the most
Everyone judges their own performance equally accurately whether they perform well or poorly
The best performers misjudge their own performance the most compared with the other groups
mcq.e: The paper: "participants who performed the best demonstrated more accurate judgments than those who performed more poorly."

mcq.q: In the Kruger and Dunning (1999) logic puzzle study, what did the bottom quartile estimate and what was reality?
o: Estimated and actual both 5 correct
Estimated 1 of 10 correct; in reality 5.5 on average
Estimated 10 of 10 correct; in reality 5.5 on average
Estimated 5.5 of 10 correct; in reality under 1 on average
mcq.e: The paper: "participants in the bottom quartile estimated that they had answered 5.5 of 10 problems correctly; in reality, they answered, on average, less than 1 problem correctly."

mcq.q: What does the "double curse of incompetence" mean?
o: Poor task knowledge hurts both performing and judging one's performance
Incompetent people must take the test twice, so they have more chances to improve their marks
Incompetent people are penalized twice on the marks they receive at the end of the course
Incompetent people are abandoned twice by the teacher, so they receive no support in class
mcq.e: The paper: "poor task knowledge also renders individuals less able to assess task performance, giving rise to... the 'double curse of incompetence'".

mcq.q: What exception does the paper note to a positive link between task knowledge and metacognitive accuracy?
o: Domain knowledge is sometimes negatively related to monitoring in text comprehension (Glenberg and Epstein)
Domain knowledge is always positively related to every metacognitive judgment in every kind of task
There is no exception of any kind, because the link between knowledge and accuracy is a law
Only children show exceptions, while in adults the link is always positive and never fails
mcq.e: The paper: "domain knowledge may sometimes be negatively related to metacognition for text comprehension... the relation is by no means lawful."

mcq.q: Which two kinds of judgment did Dougherty, Scheck, Nelson and Narens (2005) compare, and what did they find?
o: Prospective and retrospective judgments; retrospective judgments predicted later performance better
Written and spoken judgments; they found that spoken judgments were far more accurate
Individual and group judgments; they found that individual judgments were far more accurate
Fast and slow judgments; they found that fast judgments predicted later performance far better
mcq.e: The paper: "Retrospective judgment predicted subsequent test performance better than prospective judgment."

mcq.q: Why might prospective judgments be less accurate?
o: They rely on more noise and uncertainty, while retrospective judgments draw on better information since the task is done
Learners are not allowed to see the test in advance, so they have no information to judge from
Prospective judgments are always written down, so they are affected by spelling errors in writing
Prospective judgments are always made faster than retrospective ones and so are less careful
mcq.e: The paper: "prospective judgments necessarily rely on more noise and uncertainty than retrospective judgments, which provide access to better information, given that the judge has completed the task."

mcq.q: According to Koriat's (1997) cue-utilization framework, when are predictions of learning accurate?
o: When the learner has many friends who confirm that the lesson has been well mastered
When the learner makes the judgment as fast as possible without weighing any other cues
When the cues used at judgment time are consistent with the factors that affect later performance
When the learner uses no cues at all and relies on a general feeling about the material
mcq.e: The paper: predictions "are accurate as long as the cues used at the time of making the judgments are consistent with the factors that affect subsequent performance on the criterion memory test."

mcq.q: How many word pairs did participants study in Nelson and Dunlosky (1991)?
o: 52 pairs
66 unrelated pairs
100 pairs
16 pairs
mcq.e: The paper: "a list of 66 unrelated paired associates (e.g., TABLE-SPOON)".

mcq.q: What g values did delayed and immediate predictions have in Nelson and Dunlosky?
o: Both were g = .38
Delayed g = .38; immediate g = .90
Both were g = .90
Delayed g = .90; immediate g = .38
mcq.e: The paper: "Delaying predictions resulted in highly accurate predictions (g = .90) compared with immediate predictions (g = .38)."

mcq.q: Why were delayed predictions more accurate?
o: Delay made learners forget the content, so they relied only on random guesses about their memory
Delay let learners sleep longer, so their minds were clearer when they had to make the judgments
Delay encouraged retrieval from long-term memory
Delay made the final test easier, so predictions were more likely to coincide with the results
mcq.e: The paper: "delaying judgment encouraged participants to attempt to retrieve the studied item; the success or failure of that retrieval is highly diagnostic of future learning outcomes."

mcq.q: When judgments are made immediately, what do participants rely on?
o: The scores of classmates, from which they infer how well they are likely to do themselves
Only what is currently accessible, which impedes accuracy
The results of the test in the future that they already know from earlier attempts at the task
The direct advice of the teacher about how well they are going to do on the coming test
mcq.e: The paper: "participants relied only on what was currently accessible as a basis for prediction, impeding accuracy when the judgment called for a prediction of future test performance."

mcq.q: What classroom activity does Rhodes suggest to separate immediate performance from long-lasting learning?
o: Assigning more homework so that students have more time to practice at home each night
Abolishing all quizzes so that students do not confuse performance with lasting learning
A short quiz right after a lecture and a delayed quiz, then discussing the difference
Having students copy the lecture many times so that the content is fixed in memory better
mcq.e: The paper: instructors could "manipulate the timing of class quizzes... A failure to appreciate this distinction can have significant consequences for metacognition".

mcq.q: What are the three classroom activities Rhodes suggests?
o: Taking notes, writing lines as punishment and memorizing the most important parts of lectures
Watching films, listening to music and playing games to relax after long and tiring lessons
Watching poor television auditions, predicting and postdicting exam scores, and delayed testing
Competing between groups, ranking students by score and rewarding those who come out top
mcq.e: The paper: "American Idol and Metacognitive Awareness", "Predicting Exam Performance" and "Delayed Testing".

mcq.q: Why does Rhodes stress the accuracy of metacognition in teaching?
o: Students' assessments of learning determine how they prepare for exams, so illusions of learning must be avoided
Because metacognition has no effect at all on how students prepare for their important exams
Because accurate metacognition makes students less confident and therefore worse at exams
Because metacognition is always accurate, teachers need only teach more content without adjusting it
mcq.e: The paper: "their ongoing assessments of learning (i.e., monitoring)... will determine how they go about preparing for exams... it is imperative that students' metacognition is accurate and not subject to illusions of learning."

mcq.q: What does Rhodes suggest doing to improve students' metacognition?
o: Withhold grades after an exam so that students are not influenced by the result of the previous test
Increase task knowledge and create environments with high-quality cues that reveal mastery
Forbid students to predict their own scores because predicting only makes them anxious and distracted
Give students less time on exams so that they must work fast and cannot stop to doubt themselves
mcq.e: The paper: "gaining task knowledge and creating learning environments where high-quality cues accurately disclose mastery (e.g., engaging in extensive self-testing) will enhance metacognition".

mcq.q: Why should you not rely on MAI scores alone to conclude about students' monitoring accuracy?
o: Because the MAI has no items at all about monitoring comprehension while reading or studying
Because the MAI was designed only for elementary school children and does not fit university students
In Experiment 2, the MAI was not significantly related to monitoring accuracy
Because the MAI always gives the same score to every participant, so it cannot tell people apart
mcq.e: Schraw and Dennison found no statistical relationship between monitoring accuracy and the MAI, so measuring "knowing what you know" needs confidence and real-outcome data as well.

mcq.q: Why does measuring calibration require both confidence and the actual result for each person?
o: Because calibration is simply the score of the test that the learner earned on that occasion
Because calibration needs only confidence, without knowing how many the learner actually got right
Because calibration never changes over time, so it needs to be measured only one single time
Calibration is the correspondence between judgment and performance
mcq.e: Rhodes defines accuracy as the correspondence between judgment and performance; both Foster and Schraw–Dennison compute it from two-sided data (confidence and actual score).

mcq.q: Which of these is a misconception about metacognition?
o: "High metacognition always goes with high intellectual ability or achievement"
"Monitoring affects control, so wrong monitoring can lead to wrong study decisions"
"Metacognition can be taught, practiced and improved as time goes by in a learner"
"Metacognition can be accurate or inaccurate, and its accuracy can change over time"
mcq.e: Schraw and Dennison (citing Swanson 1990, Pressley and Ghatala 1990) say metacognition appears independent of intellectual ability and academic achievement.

mcq.q: Why are weak students often the most overconfident, according to the Schraw–Dennison and Rhodes data?
o: The low group had the highest monitoring inaccuracy (overconfidence)
Because they do not do the test, so they merely guess their confidence with no basis at all
Because they always know the correct answers, so they need not weigh their confidence carefully
Because they study more than the other students, so they have grounds to be more certain about results
mcq.e: Schraw–Dennison: the low group M = .28 was the most overconfident; Rhodes: "poor task knowledge also renders individuals less able to assess task performance".

mcq.q: In the thesis, what data are needed to ask whether students' confidence in understanding AI-written code matches their score without AI?
o: Only the number of lines of code the AI wrote for students when they asked questions in class
Only the number of times students logged in to the learning system during the whole term
Only a questionnaire score about students' attitudes toward AI before and after the programming course
Students' confidence before a no-AI test and their actual score on that test
mcq.e: A design inference based on Rhodes's definition of calibration (confidence versus performance) for RQ2; not a result from any study.

mcq.q: Which statement is a design hypothesis (not a conclusion of the paper) when linking Rhodes to AI?
o: Rhodes concluded that students should not use AI because it causes illusions of learning in everyone
Rhodes measured the calibration of students who used AI to write code for programming assignments
Fluent AI-written code may create cues that make students feel they understand, like the loudness illusion
Rhodes proved experimentally that AI reduces the metacognition of the students who use it
mcq.e: Rhodes (2019) does not discuss AI; the link is a design hypothesis based on the cue mechanism that produces illusions.

mcq.q: From Rhodes, which components could go into a "responsible AI" intervention?
o: Having students reread the answers given by the AI many times so they remember the content better
Asking for predictions and postdictions, delayed self-testing, and feedback on calibration error
Hiding scores from students so they are not influenced by the results of earlier assignments
Making students memorize the source code written by the AI to be sure they remember how to do it
mcq.e: Rhodes suggests predicting and postdicting scores against actual scores, and delayed testing; this is a design inference for the treatment.

mcq.q: How should Liles (2000) be used in this module?
o: Only as a short book review with one defining paragraph
As the main source about the structure of the metacognition model in modern theory
As strong empirical evidence of the effectiveness of metacognitive training programs
As a standard metacognition scale that can be used directly in your own thesis
mcq.e: Liles (2000) is a book review in Physiotherapy that states briefly that metacognition is "the knowledge of one's own thought processes".

mcq.q: Which is a reasonable way to measure metacognition in RQ2 while avoiding the limits of questionnaires?
o: Use only the final exam score because it already reflects monitoring ability fully
Combine an MAI-type questionnaire with calibration computed from confidence
Use a single question such as "do you know what you know" and score it from 1 to 5
Use only self-reported study hours because study hours reflect metacognition best
mcq.e: Garner–Alexander recommend multiple methods not sharing a source of error; Schraw–Dennison show the MAI did not predict monitoring accuracy (a design inference).

mcq.q: What does Flavell's caution about excessive monitoring imply for intervention design?
o: Drop every form of self-checking because it only wastes students' time and lowers learning
It has no implication for design because the caution applies only to small children
Do not make students self-check at every step until they are paralyzed; monitor selectively
Increase the number of self-checks to the maximum at every step so students always control learning
mcq.e: Flavell warns of the obsessive paralyzed by constant evaluation; this design suggestion is inferred from that caution.

essay.q: Distinguish metacognitive knowledge, metacognitive experiences, goals and strategies in Flavell's (1979) model and give one programming-learning example of each.
essay.m: Hint: Knowledge: beliefs about person, task, strategy (for example "I debug better by printing intermediate values"). Experiences: conscious feelings (for example suddenly sensing you do not understand nested loops). Goals: the aim of the task (make the program pass three test cases). Strategies: cognitive (reread the task, rewrite the function) and metacognitive (ask yourself questions to check understanding). Show that they interact: experiences trigger strategies and update knowledge. The examples are design inference.

essay.q: Describe the two components and eight subcomponents of metacognition in Schraw and Dennison (1994). What evidence supports the two-component model, and what evidence fails to support eight?
essay.m: Hint: Knowledge of cognition (declarative, procedural, conditional); regulation of cognition (planning, information management, monitoring, debugging, evaluation). Unrestricted analysis gave six factors (78% of variance) that did not match eight, alphas .81 to .59; forced two factors gave alpha .91, .95 overall, r = .54, replicated in Experiment 2 (alphas .88, .88; r = .45).

essay.q: Explain the difference between calibration and resolution in Rhodes (2019) and give a way to compute each from students' confidence and actual scores.
essay.m: Hint: Calibration (absolute accuracy): signed or absolute difference between mean confidence and proportion correct; calibration curve by confidence bins. Example Foster: 84.44 minus 77.69, about 6.75 points overconfident. Resolution (relative accuracy): correlation (Goodman–Kruskal gamma) between item-level confidence and correct/incorrect; Koriat and Goldsmith g = .87. State the limitation: calibration changes when actual performance changes.

essay.q: Analyze the loudness illusion experiment of Rhodes and Castel (2009) and draw implications for students using AI when learning programming.
essay.m: Hint: Learners predicted better recall for loud words but recall did not differ; they chose to restudy normal words nearly twice as often: an illusion in monitoring led to a wrong control decision. Implication (design hypothesis): clear, fluent AI-written code may be a cue that makes students think they understand; measure calibration on no-AI tests and give feedback on the error.

essay.q: Evaluate the limits of the evidence in Schraw and Dennison (1994) and Garner and Alexander (1989), then propose how to supplement them when measuring metacognition in your thesis.
essay.m: Hint: Schraw–Dennison: educational psychology undergraduates, self-report, the MAI did not predict monitoring accuracy, dated 1994. Garner–Alexander: a review posing questions, not an experiment; problems with interview measures. Supplement: combine the MAI with calibration (item-level confidence versus correctness), collect behavioral traces during the task (self-tests, time before asking the AI), think-aloud on a subsample, and report limits transparently.

essay.q: According to Garner and Alexander (1989), why are well-taught strategies often abandoned? Name the three groups of factors (procedural, attributional, contextual) and apply them to teaching programming with AI.
essay.m: Hint: Procedural: match strategy to task, modeling, guided practice, self-control training. Attributional: Nicholls (task-involved versus ego-involved); attributing failure to low ability leads to giving up. Contextual: performance versus mastery classrooms (Ames and Archer 1988, 176 students). Application: design a class with mastery feedback, allow errors and revision, avoid competitive ranking, and explain clearly when AI use is appropriate. This is design inference.
